questions.q: What is the purpose of the kid header in a JWT?
o: It records the username of the user who originally issued the token
It tells the server which signing key to use for verification
It stores the token expiration as a compact header string
It identifies the JWT library version that created the token
questions.x: kid stands for Key ID. It is an optional header used when a server manages multiple signing keys. The server reads kid and looks up the matching key, from a database or from the filesystem.
questions.h: A server may have more than one signing key. What question does kid answer for that server?

questions.q: When does kid become vulnerable to path traversal?
o: When the server uses kid as a filesystem path without sanitizing it
When signing keys are stored only in a database by identifier
When kid is copied from the JWT header into payload claims
When the token uses RS256 so keys never touch the filesystem
questions.x: Directory traversal is possible when kid is used to fetch a key file and the value is not sanitized. An attacker can supply ../ sequences and point the lookup at a file whose contents they already know.
questions.h: Path traversal needs user input inside a file path. Where does a vulnerable server put the kid value?

questions.q: Why is /dev/null a useful target for kid path traversal?
o: Reading it crashes authentication by panicking the kernel
Reading it prints the real signing key in an error message
Reading it returns empty content, so the HMAC key is empty
Writing to it overwrites the live key file used by the server
questions.x: On Linux, /dev/null always returns empty content. The server then uses an empty string as the signing key. The attacker signs the forged JWT with the same empty string, so the signatures match.
questions.h: The attacker must know exactly what key the server will load. What file has completely predictable empty contents?

questions.q: Which statement about the kid header is correct?
o: kid selects the verification key
Unsanitized kid can be a file path
/dev/null yields an empty string key
All of these statements are true
questions.x: All three are true. kid tells the server which key to use. If that lookup is a raw filesystem path, traversal is possible. Pointing kid at /dev/null makes the signing key an empty string.
questions.h: Compare each option to how kid is used, and to what /dev/null returns when read.

questions.q: After pointing kid at /dev/null, how does the attacker forge a valid JWT?
o: They drop the signature and switch the alg header to none
They sign the forged token with an empty string as the HMAC secret
They copy the original signature onto a new payload unchanged
They encrypt the new payload using the contents of /dev/null
questions.x: The server loads empty content from /dev/null and uses that empty string as the HS256 key. Signing the attacker payload with the same empty string produces a signature the server will accept.
questions.h: The server and the attacker must use the same HMAC key. What is that key after a /dev/null read?
